title: Why Do You Stand Far Off? The Arrogance of the Wicked
summary: The psalm opens with a blunt question: why does the LORD stand far off when the poor are hunted? It paints a long portrait of the wicked man who boasts, sneers, ambushes the helpless, and tells himself that God will never see. Then it calls on God to arise, confesses that he does see, and ends with confidence in the LORD as King forever, the helper of the fatherless and the oppressed.
story: Psalm 10 completes the poem that began in Psalm 9. There the psalmist praised God for past justice and said the needy would not always be forgotten. Here the present looks very different: God seems absent, and the wicked prosper by preying on the weak. The pair teaches readers to hold memory and complaint together. It is not only individual enemies that trouble the psalmist now, but a whole pattern of social injustice, in which the powerful exploit the powerless and assume there is no one to call them to account. The psalm pushes the question of Book 1 (does God really protect the righteous?) into the public square.
historical:
Psalm 10 has no heading of its own, which is unusual among Psalms 3 to 41; only Psalms 1, 2, 10, and 33 lack one in this first book. Together with the continuation of the broken acrostic pattern from Psalm 9, this is the main evidence that Psalms 9 and 10 were originally one poem, as the Septuagint and Vulgate treat them. If so, the attribution to David in Psalm 9's heading covers Psalm 10 as well. Scholars who favor a later date for much of the Psalter note that the psalm's focus on the exploited poor and on a practical atheism among the powerful resembles the social critique of the eighth-century prophets such as Amos, Micah, and Isaiah. The text itself names no rulers or events.

What can be said with confidence is the kind of world the psalm assumes: villages exposed to raiders and predatory landowners, weak legal protection for the poor, and powerful men who used courts, debt, and violence to take what they wanted. The Old Testament laws and prophets repeatedly condemn exactly those abuses.
cultural:
The victims in this psalm are the needy, the helpless, the lowly, the oppressed, and the fatherless. In ancient Israel, as in its neighbors, a person's security depended on family and land. The fatherless (often with their widowed mothers) had lost the male protector who represented them in court and held the family's land. Israel's law set God himself as their defender (Exodus 22:22-24; Deuteronomy 10:18), and the kings of the ancient Near East, including in the Babylonian law code of Hammurabi, claimed to protect the widow and the orphan. Psalm 10 appeals to God as the king who actually does it.

The images are drawn from rural life and hunting. The wicked lies in ambush near the villages, the small unwalled settlements outside towns. He lurks like a lion in a thicket and catches the lowly in a net. His mouth is full of cursing and deceit, and trouble is “under his tongue”, as if held in reserve like food in the mouth. The phrase “in all his schemes there is no God” describes a practical atheism: not a philosophical denial of God's existence, which was rare in the ancient world, but a way of life that assumes God does not care or will not act.
literary: The psalm moves from lament to confidence. Verses 1 and 2 ask why God is far off. Verses 3 to 11 are a long portrait of the wicked, marked by the refrain “He says to himself” (verses 6, 11, and 13), which lets readers overhear his inner speech. Verses 12 to 15 turn with a command: “Arise, O LORD”. The psalmist answers the wicked man's claims one by one: he says God never sees, but “You have regarded trouble and grief”. Verses 16 to 18 close in confident praise of the LORD as King forever. The word “forget” links the two psalms: the nations forget God (9:17), the wicked claims God has forgotten (10:11), and the psalmist asks God not to forget the helpless (10:12).

outline.t: Why do you stand far off?
The pride and speech of the wicked
The wicked as hunter: God never sees
Arise, O LORD: you do see
The LORD is King and helper of the fatherless

doctrines.note: The psalm begins with the question every sufferer asks: why is God far away when evil prospers? It does not answer the question with a theory, but it keeps the question inside prayer.
The wicked man's root sin is pride that shuts God out: he does not seek God and tells himself there is no judge. Violence against the weak grows from that inner denial.
Against every appearance, “The LORD is King forever and ever”. His kingship shows itself in hearing the humble and defending the fatherless.

words.note: Yatom, fatherless or orphan. It describes a child who has lost a father and so lost protection, provision, and legal standing. In verses 14 and 18 God is the helper and vindicator of the fatherless. Throughout the Old Testament, how a society treats the fatherless is a test of its faithfulness to God.

Anav, humble or poor. The word joins material poverty with a lowly spirit, people who have no power and depend on God. Verse 17 says God has heard their desire. It is close to the word behind Jesus' blessing on the meek (Matthew 5:5, echoing Psalm 37:11).

Darash, to seek or inquire. It appears three times in this psalm. The wicked does not seek God (verse 4); he thinks God will not seek out (call to account) his wickedness (verse 13); but the psalmist asks God to seek it out until none is left (verse 15). The same verb describes both prayer and judgment.

christ: Paul quotes verse 7 in Romans 3:14, in the same chain of texts that includes Psalm 5:9 and Psalm 14, to show that the speech of sinful humanity is full of cursing and bitterness. The psalm's hope, that the LORD is King and hears the humble, is announced in the Gospels as the arrival of God's kingdom in Jesus, who blesses the poor and the meek. James, the brother of Jesus, speaks of pure religion as caring for orphans and widows in their distress (James 1:27), carrying the psalm's concern into the church. These are thematic connections. Christians also see in the question “Why do You stand far off?” a cry that Jesus himself took up from another psalm on the cross (Psalm 22:1), entering the experience of God's seeming absence.

hard.q: Why does God seem to hide while the wicked prosper?
hard.a: The psalm doesn't pretend otherwise. It opens by accusing God of standing far off, and it lets the wicked man's boast (“He hides His face and never sees”) stand in the text. The Bible offers several responses across its books rather than a single formula. The psalms themselves insist that God does see and will act in his time (verse 14). Job warns against assuming we understand God's purposes. The prophets speak of God's patience, which delays judgment to allow repentance. The New Testament points to the cross, where God was present in apparent absence, and to a final judgment where every hidden wrong is brought to light. What the psalm models is not an explanation but a posture: bringing the question to God, naming the injustice honestly, and holding on to his kingship.

questions: The psalm begins with “Why?” When has God seemed far off to you, and what did you do with that question?
The wicked man in this psalm lives as though God does not see. In what small ways do people who believe in God still live as practical atheists?
God is called the helper of the fatherless. Who in your community has lost their protector, and what would it look like to stand with them?
